message.content:
Sure! If you’re looking to pull detailed information about all **nodes** in your cluster, there are several ways depending on what environment and tooling you prefer: | Tool/Method | What it does | How to run | |-------------|--------------|------------| | `kubectl` CLI | Native command‑line interface for Kubernetes – lists nodes & their status | ```bash
kubectl get nodes -o wide # basic details + IP addresses

# For full JSON/YAML output:
kubectl get nodes -o json > nodes.json``` | | REST API (`GET /api/v1/nodes`) | Direct HTTP call against kube‑apiserver – returns raw JSON | ```http GET https:///api/v1/nodes```, authenticated with bearer token or client cert. | | Client Libraries (Python) | Programmatic access – great if you want to parse/filter data | ```python\nfrom kubernetes import client, config\nconfig.load_kube_config() # uses ~/.kube/config\nv1 = client.CoreV1Api()\nprint(v1.list_node())\n``` | | Cloud provider console/API | Most managed clusters expose “Node” dashboards/APIs (GKE, EKS, AKS). | Use GCP Console → Compute Engine → Nodes, AWS ECS/EKS console, Azure Portal → Virtual Machines. | --- ### Quick Start With `kubectl` If you already have `kubectl` configured to talk to your cluster, this will give you everything you need: ```bash # Basic overview: kubectl get nodes # More detail (IP address, OS image, kernel version): kubectl get nodes -o wide # Full YAML dump (good for debugging or archiving): kubectl get nodes -o yaml > nodes.yaml ``` #### Example Output ``` NAME STATUS ROLES AGE VERSION ip-192-168-0-5 Ready control-plane,master 30d v1.28.2 ip-192-168-0-12 Ready worker 29d v1.28.2 ... ``` Each node entry contains labels such as `node-role.kubernetes.io/master=true`. You can also inspect annotations, capacity, allocatable resources, conditions, etc.: ```bash kubectl describe node ip-192-168-0-5 ``` This prints out sections like *Capacity*, *Allocatable*, *Conditions* (Ready, DiskPressure, MemoryPressure), *Labels*, *Annotations*, and more. --- ### Using the REST API Manually For scripting without `kubectl`, just hit the `/api/v1/nodes` endpoint: ```bash curl --header "Authorization: Bearer $(cat $HOME/.kube/token)" \ --cacert $HOME/.kube/cacerts.pem \ https://$KUBERNETES_MASTER/api/v1/nodes ``` Replace `$KUBERNETES_MASTER` with your apiserver host/IP. This returns a huge JSON blob containing each node’s spec, status, metadata, etc. --- ### Pull Node Info From Code (Python) Below is a minimal script that pulls node names, statuses, and some useful metrics: ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 import os from kubernetes import client, config def main(): # Load local kube-config (~/.kube/config) config.load_kube_config() core_v1_api = client.CoreV1Api() nodes = core_v1_api.list_node().items print(f"{'NODE':20} {'STATUS':15} {'ROLES'}") print("-"*60) for n in nodes: name = n.metadata.name roles = [label.split('=')[1] for label in n.metadata.labels.keys() if label.startswith("node-role")] role_str = ",".join(roles) or "none" ready_condition = next( cond.status == "True" for cond in n.status.conditions if cond.type == "Ready", None ) status = "READY" if ready_condition else "NOT READY" print(f"{name:20} {status:15} {role_str}") if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` Run it after installing the official client library: ```bash pip install kubernetes python show_nodes.py ``` Feel free to extend the script to extract other fields—like CPU/memory capacity, allocated pods, or custom labels. --- ### Common Troubleshooting Tips | Issue | Fix | |-------|-----| | `Error from server (Forbidden): ...` | Ensure your kubeconfig has proper RBAC permissions (`cluster-admin` or at least read rights on nodes). | | TLS errors when calling API directly | Verify CA certificate path matches the one used by your cluster. | | Missing `kubectl` binary | Install via package manager (`apt-get install kubectl`, Homebrew `brew install kubectl`). | | Need node logs | Use `journalctl -u kubelet -b` on the node itself or view container runtime logs. | Let me know which method works best for you—or if you’d like help setting up authentication tokens, certificates, or parsing specific node attributes!
